passages.t: A man called Legion set free
passages.happening:
Jesus and his disciples land on the far side of the lake. As soon as Jesus steps out of the boat, a man comes running from the tombs. An unclean spirit has hold of him. People have tried to chain him, but he breaks the chains. Night and day he cries out among the tombs and hills and cuts himself with stones.

He falls at Jesus' feet and shouts, “What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?” Jesus asks his name. “My name is Legion,” he replies, “for we are many.” The spirits beg to be sent into a large herd of pigs feeding on the hillside. Jesus lets them go. The herd, about two thousand pigs, rushes down the steep bank into the lake and drowns.
passages.hearers:
For a Jewish hearer, every detail in this scene says ‘unclean’. The east side of the lake was mostly Gentile land, the territory of the Decapolis, a league of Greek cities. The law called the pig unclean (Leviticus 11:7), and later Jewish law forbade Jews to raise pigs at all. Pigs also carried a bitter memory. In the 160s BC the Greek king Antiochus IV tried to stamp out Judaism and ordered pigs to be sacrificed. Touching a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). Here is a man with an unclean spirit, living among graves, beside a herd of pigs, in Gentile country. Isaiah once described a rebellious people “sitting among the graves” and “eating the meat of pigs” (Isaiah 65:4). Jesus walks straight into the middle of all of it.

The name Legion would have struck hard. A legion was a unit of the Roman army, some five thousand soldiers, the face of Rome's power in the land. The Tenth Legion, which later fought in Judea, even had a wild boar among its badges. Some readers hear a hint about Rome in the name. Others think it simply means a vast number, as the spirit itself explains. Either way, the man is held by something like an army.

The place itself is a puzzle. Mark says ‘the region of the Gerasenes’, but the city of Gerasa lay some thirty miles from the lake. Old copies of the Gospels read Gerasenes, Gadarenes, or Gergesenes, which shows that early scribes felt the difficulty. In the 200s the scholar Origen pointed to a town called Gergesa on the shore. At Kursi, on the east shore, a steep slope and the ruins of a large Byzantine monastery were uncovered in the 1970s, and many think this was the place, though not all agree.
passages.ot:
Just before, Jesus said that no one can rob a strong man's house unless he “first ties up the strong man” (3:27). Here is that saying acted out. No one had the strength to bind this man. Jesus binds the power that held him.

‘Most High God’ is an old name for the God of Israel, used as far back as Melchizedek, “priest of God Most High” (Genesis 14:18). The spirit knows exactly who Jesus is, which is more than the disciples did in the boat.
passages.hard:
Was this man possessed by spirits, or was he mentally ill, described in the language of his time? Mark presents a real spiritual power that speaks, bargains, and leaves. Many modern readers think of illness instead. Christians have answered in more than one way. Many hold that both are real: that most suffering of the mind is illness, to be met with medicine and care, and that the Bible also speaks of evil powers that are more than illness. Most warn strongly against treating every illness as a demon. Mark's point is not to give a diagnosis. It is that nothing that holds a person, however strong, is stronger than Jesus.

The man was harming himself. If that is where you or someone you love is today, please reach out for real help now, to a doctor, a pastor, or a crisis line.
passages.asks: Notice who Jesus crosses a stormy lake to reach: one man, alone, unclean, chained, and beyond anyone's help. Ask who in your world has been written off as too far gone, and what it would mean to believe that Jesus would cross a lake for them. Ask also what holds you that you cannot break.

passages.happening:
The men looking after the pigs run and tell everyone in the town and the countryside. People come out to see. They find the man sitting quietly, dressed, and in his right mind. And they are afraid. They beg Jesus to leave.

As Jesus gets back into the boat, the healed man begs to go with him. Jesus says no. “Go home to your own people,” He said, “and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and what mercy He has shown you.” The man goes and tells people all over the Decapolis what Jesus has done, and everyone is amazed.
passages.hearers:
Two things would have surprised a first hearer. First, the people are more afraid of the calm man than they ever were of the wild one. They had learned to live with a madman in chains. They did not know how to live with a power that could undo him, and that cost them a herd.

Second, Jesus tells this man to speak. In Jewish Galilee Jesus has told people to keep quiet (1:44). Here, in Gentile land, he sends a man home to tell what happened. The Decapolis was a league of Greek cities, Greek in language and in worship. The first person Jesus sends to that world is a man who had lived among the tombs.

Notice the wording too. Jesus tells him to tell what ‘the Lord’ has done. The man goes and tells what ‘Jesus’ has done. Mark lets the reader notice that the two are spoken of as one.
passages.hard: Why did Jesus let the spirits destroy about two thousand pigs, and the owners' living with them? Mark does not say, and it is wise not to claim too much. Some point out that Jesus only gave permission and that the destruction was the work of the spirits, showing what they had meant to do to the man. Others say the drowned herd was visible proof, to the man and the town, that the spirits were truly gone. Others see a sign that Jesus treats one human life as worth more than a herd. Many readers also feel the cost for the owners, and it is honest to admit that the passage does not answer every question it raises.
passages.asks: The people of the town asked Jesus to leave because his power cost them something. Ask whether there is any part of your life where you have quietly asked Jesus to stay away because his coming would be costly. And notice that the healed man's first task was at home, with the people who knew him at his worst.

passages.t: A father begs for his daughter
passages.happening: Jesus crosses back to the Jewish side of the lake, and a large crowd gathers. A synagogue leader named Jairus comes and falls at his feet. “My little daughter is near death,” he begs. “Please come and place Your hands on her, so that she will be healed and live.” Jesus goes with him, and the crowd presses in on every side.
passages.hearers:
A synagogue leader was an important man in a Jewish town. He looked after the meeting place where people gathered each Sabbath to hear the Scriptures read and taught. In Acts, synagogue leaders are the ones who invite a visitor to speak (Acts 13:15). Jairus had standing, a home, and a name people knew.

So it would have been striking to see him on the ground at the feet of a travelling teacher. Some religious leaders were already wary of Jesus: in Mark 3 he was watched in a synagogue to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath. Jairus sets all of that aside. A dying child makes a father forget his position.
passages.asks: Jairus came because he had nowhere else to go. His need was greater than his pride. Ask what you would do if your standing, your reputation, or your caution stood between you and asking Jesus for help. What would it take for you to fall at his feet?

passages.t: The woman who touched his cloak
passages.happening:
In the crowd is a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years. She has suffered under many doctors and spent everything she had, and she has only grown worse. She has heard about Jesus. She thinks, “If only I touch His garments, I will be healed.” She comes up behind him and touches his cloak. At once the bleeding stops, and she can feel in her body that she is healed.

Jesus knows that power has gone out from him. He turns and asks who touched him. His disciples think the question is silly, with so many people pushing against him. But he keeps looking. Trembling, the woman comes forward, falls at his feet, and tells him the whole truth. He calls her ‘Daughter’ and tells her, “your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction.”
passages.hearers:
Her illness touched every part of her life. Under the law of Moses, a woman with a long flow of blood was ritually unclean for as long as it lasted, and anything she lay or sat on became unclean too (Leviticus 15:25-27). ‘Unclean’ here does not mean sinful or dirty. It meant she could not come near to worship at the temple, and people who touched her things had to wash. Scholars debate how cut off from daily life this made her. But twelve years of illness, of being careful who she touched, and of paying doctors who could not help, would have worn down anyone.

That is why she comes from behind and says nothing. By the law's rules, her touch should have made Jesus unclean. Instead, as with the leper in chapter 1, the flow goes the other way. His power makes her well.

Then Jesus calls her ‘Daughter’. It is the only time in Mark that he calls anyone by that name. A woman who had been on the edge for twelve years is named in front of the whole crowd as one who belongs.
passages.hard: Why did Jesus make her come forward? She was already healed, and she was afraid. It can look harsh. But if she had slipped away, she would have had her body healed and nothing more. By calling her out, Jesus lets the crowd see that she is clean. He gives her his word of peace, not just his power. And he names what happened: it was not magic in his cloak but her trust in him that he honours.
passages.asks: She came hoping to get help without being seen. Jesus wanted more for her than that. Ask whether you come to God hoping for help while keeping your distance. What would it mean to come forward and tell him “the whole truth”?

passages.t: The girl who was not dead but asleep
passages.happening:
While Jesus is still speaking to the woman, messengers arrive from Jairus's house. “Your daughter is dead,” they say. There is no need to trouble the teacher any longer. Jesus hears and says to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just believe.”

He takes only Peter, James, and John. At the house the mourners are weeping and wailing. Jesus asks why they are making such a noise: the child is not dead but asleep. They laugh at him. He sends them all out, takes the parents and his three disciples into the room, and takes the girl by the hand. “Talitha koum!” he says, which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!” At once she gets up and walks around. She is twelve years old. Jesus tells them to keep it quiet and to give her something to eat.
passages.hearers:
Mourning began at once when someone died. Families hired flute players and women who wailed. A rule recorded in the Mishnah, the collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, says that even a poor man must provide at least two flute players and one wailing woman for his wife's funeral. The noise at Jairus's house was what people expected. And the mourners' laughter shows they had no doubt the girl was dead.

‘Talitha koum’ is Aramaic, the everyday language of Jesus' home. ‘Talitha’ is a tender word for a little girl; ‘koum’ means ‘get up’. Mark keeps the very words and then translates them for his Greek-speaking readers. These may be the exact sounds the parents heard.

The delay matters too. Mark tells this story in two halves, with the woman's healing in the middle. While Jesus stopped for her, the girl died. Both are called ‘daughter’. The woman had been ill for twelve years. The girl was twelve years old. One story helps us read the other.
passages.ot: The prophets Elijah and Elisha each brought a dead boy back to life (1 Kings 17:17-24; 2 Kings 4:32-37). Elisha shut the door, prayed, and stretched himself over the boy again and again. Elijah cried out, “O LORD my God, please let this boy’s life return to him!” (1 Kings 17:21). Jesus also clears the room. But he does not pray for the child's life to return. He takes her hand and tells her to get up.
passages.hard: Jesus says the girl is “not dead, but asleep.” Was she only in a coma? Mark does not mean that. The messengers say she is dead, the mourners are sure of it, and the point of the story is that Jesus raised her. Calling death ‘sleep’ was a way of speaking about death from God's side. For Jesus, death is something a person can be woken from. For the same reason Paul speaks of Christians who have died as “those who sleep in death” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
passages.asks: Between the bad news and the miracle, Jesus gives Jairus one sentence: “Do not be afraid; just believe.” He does not explain or promise how it will turn out. Ask where you are hearing the messengers' voice right now, saying ‘why bother?’, and what it would mean to keep walking with Jesus anyway. Notice the last detail as well: Jesus remembers that a girl who has been ill needs something to eat.
